title: 3-colorability of diameter-two graphs
formal: Does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every finite simple connected undirected graph \(G\) of diameter at most \(2\), decides whether \(G\) has a proper vertex coloring with three colors? The input does not promise that such a coloring exists. Precisely, there must be one Turing machine and constants \(C>0,b\in\mathbb N\), independent of the graph, whose worst-case running time on every valid \(n\)-vertex graph is at most \(C(n+1)^b\), and whose output is correct on every such graph.
definitions: For \(n\ge1\), the vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input is the ordinary binary encoding of \(n\), a delimiter, and an \(n\times n\) matrix of bits in row order. Valid graph matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal; a one in position \((u,v)\) means that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge. Edges are unweighted, and distance is the number of edges in a shortest path. The graph is connected if every pair has a path, and its diameter is the maximum distance over all vertex pairs; a singleton has diameter zero. A proper three-coloring is a map \(c:[n]\to\{1,2,3\}\) satisfying \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) whenever \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge; use of fewer than three colors is permitted. The decision output is one exactly when the input is a connected graph of diameter at most two admitting such a map, and zero otherwise. Malformed encodings, nonsimple graph matrices, disconnected graphs and graphs of larger diameter are rejected. Thus the problem is a total language; checking the structural promise does not change its polynomial-time classification. The machine has one finite deterministic program, ordinary finite-alphabet tapes, no oracle or advice, and no random choices. Costs include reading the explicit adjacency matrix and writing the answer, and are worst-case over all encodings with the given vertex count. There are no vertex lists, precolored vertices, restrictions on degrees, triangle exclusions or four-cycle exclusions. The number of colors and the diameter bound are fixed, while the number of vertices is unbounded. The source’s diameter-exactly-two version has the same polynomial-time question, because connected graphs of diameter zero or one are complete and constitute a polynomial-time decidable additional class.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that this total language belongs to deterministic polynomial time, or prove that it does not. A positive answer must specify a uniform algorithm and prove its worst-case polynomial bound and exact correctness on all permitted graphs, including those with no proper three-coloring. A negative answer must rule out every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. An NP-completeness theorem is a meaningful conventional hardness classification, but by itself gives a negative answer only under the additional assumption \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\); it is not an unconditional proof of nonmembership in \(\mathrm P\). A subexponential upper bound or an algorithm on a narrower forbidden-subgraph class does not settle the stated target.
why: Three-colorability is a basic constraint-satisfaction problem, and diameter is one of the simplest measures of graph connectivity. This single unresolved boundary tests whether very short distances enforce exploitable structure without any sparsity assumption. Either an algorithm or a hardness reduction would explain a fundamental limit of structural restrictions in graph algorithms.

importance.reason: A longstanding concrete tractability boundary for a canonical NP-complete problem: two colors and diameter one are easy, while three colors at diameter three are hard. It supports the broader study of algorithms on structurally restricted graphs.

progress.text: Mertzios and Spirakis give a \(2^{O(\sqrt{n\log n})}\)-time diameter-two algorithm and NP-completeness at diameter three. The 2021 paper recalls these results in its introductory classification.
Paulusma’s Section 4.3 records the unrestricted diameter-two three-color question separately from additional restricted-graph questions.
Dębski et al., Theorem 3, improve the diameter-two list-coloring time to \(2^{O(n^{1/3}\log^2 n)}\); the journal publication follows in 2022.
Murakami’s arXiv v2 proves a polynomial-time result with a four-cycle subgraph exclusion and explicitly retains the unrestricted case as open.

status_note: The unrestricted problem is explicitly left open in Murakami’s 1 July 2026 primary preprint, and bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no subsequent general resolution. The preprint’s special-case proof is not independently certified here; its four-cycle exclusion does not apply to the present unrestricted domain.

context_blocks.text: Paulusma’s 2019 open-problem discussion identifies three colors and diameter two as the outstanding tractability boundary. The same section contains further questions with extra graph restrictions or a variable number of colors. Those are distinct targets; this card keeps the existing unrestricted three-color decision problem.

The boundary is striking because diameter-one connected graphs are complete, whereas three-colorability is NP-complete already for diameter-three graphs, including triangle-free inputs. Requiring every pair of vertices to be at distance at most two leaves considerable global structure available, and its effect on the fixed three-color decision problem remains unresolved in the checked sources.

Dębski, Piecyk and Rzążewski’s Theorem 3 gives a \(2^{O(n^{1/3}\log^2 n)}\)-time algorithm for list three-coloring of diameter-two graphs, and hence for ordinary three-colorability. The statement is subexponential, not polynomial. No methods from its proof are part of the problem’s answer requirements.

Murakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list three-coloring when the graph has diameter two and contains no four-cycle as a subgraph. Its introduction and conclusion explicitly leave the unrestricted diameter-two case open. Forbidding a four-cycle as a subgraph is stronger than excluding only induced four-cycles, and neither restriction is present in this target.

category_assignment.reason: The question is polynomial-time 3-colorability on diameter-two graphs, a static algorithmic classification of a graph class.

sentences: The problem asks whether three-colorability is decidable in deterministic polynomial time for every graph of diameter at most two.
The graph is given explicitly, and it is not promised to be colorable.
No sparsity, forbidden-cycle, degree or vertex-list restriction is imposed.
The best general bound identified in the checked sources is subexponential, while a July 2026 polynomial-time result needs an additional four-cycle exclusion.
The question isolates a precise structural boundary between easy complete graphs and the known hardness at diameter three.
